howto.name: Meet the basic requirements
howto.text: Be at least 18 with a high school diploma or equivalent and a U.S. Social Security number.

howto.name: Complete the 63-hour pre-license course
howto.text: Finish Florida's state-approved 63-hour sales associate pre-license course and pass its end-of-course exam.

howto.name: Get fingerprinted
howto.text: Submit electronic fingerprints through a state-approved vendor for your background check.

howto.name: Apply to the DBPR
howto.text: Apply to the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation and receive your exam authorization.

howto.name: Pass the Florida state exam
howto.text: Pass the 100-question Florida sales associate exam (75% or higher) at a Pearson VUE testing center.

howto.name: Activate your license under a broker
howto.text: Join a licensed Florida broker, such as Adams, Cameron & Co., to activate your license and start working.

DeLand is the historic seat of Volusia County, home to Stetson University, a celebrated downtown, and a more affordable inland market that's been steadily growing. Here's exactly how to get licensed, and what the local market looks like for a new agent.

How do you get a real estate license in DeLand?

You earn the Florida real estate sales associate license, valid statewide. There is no separate DeLand license. Be 18+ with a high school diploma, complete the 63-hour pre-license course, get fingerprinted, apply to the DBPR, pass the state exam (75% to pass), and activate under a broker. Most people finish in two to four months. Full detail is in our Florida licensing guide.

Is DeLand a good market for a new real estate agent?

Yes, especially for an agent who wants an affordable, community-driven inland market rather than the coast. DeLand pairs a historic, award-winning downtown and Stetson University with newer family neighborhoods in West Volusia, drawing buyers priced out of the beachside and families wanting more home for the money. Across Volusia County, roughly 900 homes sell each month at about a $343,000 median, and West Volusia's relative affordability keeps demand steady.

Why DeLand calls itself the “Athens of Florida,” and why that matters to an agent

City founder Henry DeLand gave the town that nickname in the 1880s, reflecting his ambition to build an educational and cultural center, not just another Florida rail town. That ambition became real: DeLand's downtown is a certified Main Street district recognized nationally for its preservation, and the city carries a genuine cultural identity distinct from the beach towns 25 minutes east. For a new agent, that translates into a buyer who's often choosing DeLand deliberately, for the walkable downtown, the historic housing stock, and the small-college-town feel, not just settling for whatever's affordable. That's a different, often easier conversation than competing purely on price.

The Stetson University effect on the local market

Stetson, founded in 1883, was the first private university chartered in Florida and still anchors the west side of downtown with roughly 3,700 students, faculty, and staff who need somewhere to live. That creates a real, ongoing rental and starter-home market around campus that a beach-market agent never sees: off-campus student housing, faculty and staff relocations, and alumni who fall for the town during four years here and come back later to buy. Working DeLand well means understanding this rhythm, not just the general Volusia numbers.

DeLand's historic district: a real skill, not just a selling point

More than 600 DeLand properties sit on the local or National Register of Historic Places, concentrated in the Garden District's 1880s-to-1920s Victorian and bungalow homes. Selling and listing historic property is genuinely different work: buyers ask about preservation-district renovation rules, older systems and roofs price differently in an inspection, and sellers want an agent who can speak to a home's actual history, not just its square footage. Agents who build real expertise here have a durable niche few brand-new agents in a purely modern-construction market ever develop. Newer buyers looking for less upkeep tend toward Victoria Park, the newer-construction neighborhood east of Stetson, so DeLand genuinely spans both ends of the buyer spectrum in one town.

DeLand is growing, and it's the county seat

DeLand's population has grown meaningfully since the 2020 census, adding real, steady demand on top of its historic core. As the seat of Volusia County government, DeLand also carries a base of courthouse-adjacent legal, government, and professional employment that beach towns don't have, which tends to produce steadier, less seasonal buying and selling activity than a purely tourism- or retiree-driven market.

Does the brokerage you start with matter?

More than the town you pick. Your license must be held by a broker, and that brokerage decides your training, tools, and support in the make-or-break first year. A recognized local name carries real weight. Sellers trust it before you say a word.

Why start your real estate career with Adams, Cameron & Co.?

Adams, Cameron & Co. has been the area's largest brokerage since 1963, with a West Volusia office on South Woodland Boulevard in DeLand and around 300 agents across Volusia and Flagler County. New agents get in-house marketing at no cost, seven-day non-competing manager support, structured training, and the global Leading Real Estate Companies of the World referral network.

What is your next step?

Read the licensing guide, see the neighborhoods worth knowing in our DeLand neighborhood guide, go deeper on the town's real story in our full history of DeLand, then start a conversation with Adams, Cameron & Co. No pressure, just a clear picture of the path.

faq.q: Do I need a special license to sell real estate in DeLand?
faq.a: No. You need a Florida sales associate license, valid statewide. Complete Florida's 63-hour course, pass the state exam, clear a background check, and work locally in DeLand under a broker.

faq.q: Is DeLand a good place to start a real estate career?
faq.a: Yes. DeLand is the historic seat of Volusia County, home to Stetson University, a celebrated downtown, and a more affordable inland market that's been steadily growing. Volusia County sells about 900 homes a month, giving new agents real volume to work, especially with strong training and a recognized local brand.

faq.a: City founder Henry DeLand gave it the nickname in the 1880s to reflect his ambition to build an educational and cultural center. Stetson University, founded there in 1883, and the city's nationally recognized historic downtown are the reasons it stuck.

faq.a: Yes. With roughly 3,700 students, faculty, and staff, Stetson supports a real, ongoing off-campus rental and starter-home market around downtown, separate from the general Volusia County numbers, and alumni who lived there as students sometimes return later to buy.
